summary: This paper develops a computational model integrating Geant4/G4CMP radiation transport simulations with surface code QEC simulations to characterize how radiation-induced quasiparticle poisoning affects superconducting qubit error rates. The authors introduce a performance gap metric $\zeta_c$ to quantify QEC resilience and demonstrate that phonon downconversion via flipside Cu metallization requires increased qubit spacing (up to 4 mm from 1 mm) to fully suppress correlated errors from muon strikes on a 17-qubit [[9,1,3]] surface code.
motivation: Radiation impacts on superconducting quantum devices generate spatially and temporally correlated quasiparticle errors across multiple qubits, violating the independent error assumption underlying standard QEC codes. Previous models used phenomenological approaches with radial symmetry; a quantitative physical model is needed to properly assess error mitigation strategies and chip designs.
method: The authors map quasiparticle density evolution from Geant4/G4CMP simulations onto dynamical $T_1$ and $T_2$ times via equations (1)–(2), construct per-cycle noise models using generalized amplitude damping channels, and simulate the [[9,1,3]] surface code in Stim with minimum-weight perfect matching decoding. They sweep Cu thickness (0–13 µm) and qubit spacing (1–4 mm) on Si chips (10×10 to 40×40 mm$^2$) for 64-muon ensembles.
result: Without mitigation, muon strikes cause $p_L$ to jump immediately to ~50% loss of logical control. Cu downconversion reduces $\zeta_c$ substantially but requires qubit spacing increased to 4 mm to fully recover non-radiated performance; 500 nm Cu achieves 96% of the 13 µm film efficacy, enabling sputtering-compatible thin-film implementation. Baseline ($T_1 = 100$ µs, $T_2 = 200$ µs) logical error rates reach $\sim 10^{-3}$ per cycle without radiation.
